extracted.intended_audience: Commerce Department (BIS), federal policymakers, and manufacturing industry stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Advocacy-oriented recommendations for responding to the Commerce Department’s proposed rule restricting connected vehicles that use information and communications technology from China and Russia; focuses on balancing security and competitiveness, definitional clarity, scope, timelines, review criteria, and compliance procedures. Intended to guide notice-and-comment or stakeholder engagement with BIS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance national security, privacy, and economic strength
rubrics_metrics.description: “[N]ational security, privacy and economic strength can be pursued in conjunction with one another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking should pursue security and privacy goals while preserving economic competitiveness — i.e., adopt measures that protect national security without unduly undermining the ability of U.S. manufacturers to compete and innovate. Avoid one-dimensional approaches that sacrifice economic strength for security or vice-versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt proportionate actions that do not unduly hinder American manufacturing
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers support safeguarding efforts but “our competitiveness also requires national security challenges to be addressed through proportionate actions … [that] do not unduly hinder” American manufacturing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design restrictions and prohibitions narrowly and proportionately to the risk; consider less intrusive alternatives and exemptions where appropriate to prevent excessive disruption to production, innovation, and supply chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow sufficient time for compliance given automotive design and development cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule’s software prohibitions would go into effect for vehicles model year 2027, while the hardware regulations would take effect for vehicles model year 2030. The NAM is asking BIS to discuss with stakeholders whether they need more time to comply, given the length of the automotive design and development cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align implementation timelines with industry realities (long design/development lead times). Consult stakeholders on feasible compliance dates and consider delayed or phased compliance to avoid forcing near-term, impractical supply-chain changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and mitigate unintended consequences across the ICTS supply chain; ensure reasoned decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule in its current form could generate unintended consequences both within the automotive industry and across the broader ICTS supply chain, violating the department’s obligation to engage in reasoned decision making and avoid arbitrary and capricious rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct thorough impact analyses on downstream suppliers and the wider ICT ecosystem; identify cross-sector ripple effects and document the evidentiary basis for regulatory choices to satisfy reasoned decision-making standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clearer definitions for key terms (e.g., ‘Person Owned by, Controlled by or Subject to the Jurisdiction or Direction of a Foreign Adversary’ and ‘Connected Vehicle’)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain wording in the rule should be rephrased for clarity, including “Person Owned by, Controlled by or Subject to the Jurisdiction or Direction of a Foreign Adversary” and “Connected Vehicle.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify and narrowly tailor statutory/definition language to reduce ambiguity and compliance uncertainty. Supply concrete, operational definitions and examples so regulated entities can determine applicability without undue burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit covered software scope; avoid requiring visibility into or control over tier‑3 suppliers’ software code
rubrics_metrics.description: “[T]he NAM urges BIS to consider revising the proposed rule to ensure it does not require visibility into and control over the software code provided by an OEM’s tier 3 suppliers and beyond.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope software-related obligations to reasonable levels of supplier relationship (e.g., OEM and primary suppliers). Do not mandate intrusive access to code or proprietary information from deep-tier suppliers where that is unnecessary to mitigate security risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue clear guidance on review criteria and authorizations for approving risk assessments and mitigation measures
rubrics_metrics.description: “[T]he NAM recommends that BIS issue clear guidance about what criteria the Office of Information and Communications Technology would use to review and approve the risk assessments and the measures proposed by the applicant to mitigate the risks.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish objective, transparent criteria and procedural guidance for how OICT (or similar authority) will evaluate risk assessments and mitigation plans, including timelines, evidentiary standards, and examples of acceptable measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow attestations of compliance to protect trade secrets rather than requiring documentary disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow companies “to attest to their compliance” rather than “document and demonstrate compliance” to safeguard trade secrets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit attestations or other confidentiality-preserving compliance mechanisms when full documentary disclosure would reveal sensitive proprietary information. Establish verification/backstop procedures that balance enforcement with protection of trade secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider supplier substitution feasibility and supply-chain impacts when mandates would force new sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: If finalized, the rule would require automotive manufacturers using Chinese or Russian technology to find new suppliers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the availability, capacity, and lead times of alternative suppliers; account for industry-specific supply-chain complexity before imposing rules that effectively compel supplier changes. Consider carve-outs, transition assistance, or staged requirements where substitution is infeasible in the near term.
